steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the major points of distinction between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid):

1. Sugar Backbone  
   • DNA’s sugar is deoxyribose (lacking an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA’s sugar is ribose (has an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  

2. Nitrogenous Bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and uracil (U) instead of thymine.  

3. Strand Structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming a stable double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold into complex 3D shapes.  

4. Function  
   • DNA stores and transmits genetic information for long-term use.  
   • RNA plays various roles—messenger RNA (mRNA) carries coding instructions; transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA) help build proteins; other noncoding RNAs regulate gene expression, catalyze reactions, etc.  

5. Cellular Location  
   • DNA resides mainly in the cell nucleus (eukaryotes), and in mitochondria/chloroplasts.  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus (eukaryotes) but functions largely in the cytoplasm; in prokaryotes both DNA and RNA float together.  

6. Stability  
   • DNA’s deoxyribose and double-helix structure make it chemically very stable.  
   • RNA’s extra 2′-OH makes it more prone to hydrolysis; it’s generally short-lived and turned over rapidly.  

7. Synthesis and Processing  
   • DNA replicates via DNA polymerases, using existing strands as templates.  
   • RNA is transcribed from DNA by RNA polymerases. Eukaryotic RNA often undergoes processing (5′ capping, splicing, 3′ polyadenylation) before functioning.  

8. Types and Functions of RNA (brief overview)  
   • mRNA: carries codon sequence for protein synthesis  
   • tRNA: brings specific amino acids to the ribosome  
   • rRNA: structural and catalytic components of ribosomes  
   • snRNA, snoRNA, miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, etc.: involved in splicing, modification, regulation, and other cellular processes  

Summary  
DNA is the long-term, double-stranded archive of genetic information, built on deoxyribose and using thymine. RNA is the more versatile, single-stranded molecule—built on ribose and using uracil—tasked with relaying, regulating and even catalyzing processes that turn DNA’s instructions into functional proteins and RNAs.
